notes.meaning: Joash (also spelled Jehoash) became king of Judah as a boy of seven. He reigned forty years, as long as David and Solomon each did. His mother came from Beersheba, a town in the far south. Since he was killed at about forty-seven, he could have reigned much longer.

Joash did what was right only as long as Jehoiada the priest lived and guided him. Second Chronicles 24 tells us that after Jehoiada died, Joash turned to idols. He even had Jehoiada's son Zechariah, a prophet, put to death. It is a great gift for a young person to have wise guides, and wise to listen to them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations, such as the ESV and NRSV, read 'all his days, because Jehoiada instructed him.' Read that way, the verse could mean Joash was good his whole life.

notes.meaning: The 'high places' were local altars on hills around the country. People offered sacrifices there instead of at the temple. They were probably meant for the true God, but God's law said to sacrifice only at the place he chose. People loved these altars so much that even strong kings could not get rid of them, so the reform was only half done.

Joash wanted the temple repaired. Age had worn it down, and Athaliah's sons had damaged it on purpose. He told the priests to use three kinds of money for the work. The first was the census tax, paid by each counted man. The second was money paid to settle vows. The third was gifts people chose to give. Each priest was to collect from people he knew in his own area. Joash may have cared so much because the temple had hidden and protected him as a child.

By Joash's twenty-third year as king, the repairs still had not been done. Commentators give different reasons. Some say the priests were careless or kept the money for themselves. Others say the people did not trust the priests, or that the money all went to the priests' own living and daily worship.

The king called in Jehoiada and the priests and asked why nothing had been done. Because they had been slow, he took the handling of the money away from them. Joash was willing to correct even his old teacher when he saw the work was neglected.

The priests agreed to stop collecting the money and to stop being in charge of the repairs. They honestly admitted the job was not working in their hands, and they did not stand in the way of others doing it.

Jehoiada set up a chest with a hole in its lid. It stood at the entrance on the right side, which was the south side. Gifts for the repairs went in there, kept apart from the priests' money, and people gave more freely for a clear purpose. Once money dropped in, it could not be taken back out. Henry sees this as a picture: what we give to God should not be taken back.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that 2 Chronicles puts the chest at the gate rather than by the altar. One reads this as a compromise between the king and the priests.

notes.meaning: When the chest filled up, the king's scribe and the high priest counted the money together. They tied it up in bags. Having a royal official there alongside the priest meant no single person could be suspected, and it helped get the neglected work moving.

The counted money went to the men in charge of the work. They paid the carpenters, builders, masons and stonecutters. They also bought wood and cut stone. This happened again and again, each time the chest was emptied. The job was given to people whose trade it was, not to the priests.

While the repairs went on, none of the money was spent on fancy silver or gold dishes for the temple. All of it went to the workers. Second Chronicles 24:14 says that once the repairs were done, the leftover money was used to make such vessels. The lesson is to pay for what is most needed first.
No one checked the books of the men who paid the workers, because they had proven themselves honest. Anyone who handles church or public money should be just as faithful, knowing God sees all.

Money from the guilt offerings and sin offerings was not used for the repairs. These were offerings people brought to make up for wrongs they had done. God's law gave that money to the priests for their living. In Henry's words, the temple's servants should not be starved while the building is fixed.
Hazael, king of Aram (Syria), captured Gath, a city Judah had held since David's time. Then he set out for Jerusalem. This came after Joash had turned from God. God used Hazael to discipline him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles describe two different Syrian wars. Keil & Delitzsch argue they tell of the same war.

notes.meaning: Instead of trusting God, Joash paid Hazael off with the holy gifts and gold from the temple and the palace. Losing gold was better than losing the temple. Still, it shamed Joash and made his kingdom poorer. It also tempted Hazael to come back, which he did the next year.

More of Joash's story was written in the royal records, and some of it appears in 2 Chronicles 24. A reign that started so well ended badly, with no record that Joash ever repented. Clarke sighs, 'how few of the few who begin to live to God continue unto the end!'

Joash's own servants plotted against him and killed him. Chronicles says they did it because he had murdered Zechariah, Jehoiada's son. The killers were wrong to take revenge, yet God was just in letting it happen. Joash was buried in the City of David, but not in the royal tombs. His son Amaziah became king after him.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: One modern scholar suggests the servants may also have been unhappy after Judah's defeat by Hazael.
